title: Repentance at Mizpah: Thus Far the LORD Has Helped Us
summary: The ark stays at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years while Israel mourns and seeks the LORD. Samuel calls the people to put away their foreign gods and serve the LORD alone, and he gathers them at Mizpah to fast, confess their sin, and pray. When the Philistines attack, Samuel offers a sacrifice and cries out to the LORD, who thunders against the Philistines and routs them. Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer, and he judges Israel for the rest of his life.
story: Samuel has been absent from the story since the end of chapter 3, while the ark narrative played out. He returns here as a mature leader, and the chapter shows the kind of deliverance Israel had been hoping for in chapter 4, now achieved the right way. In chapter 4 Israel brought the ark into battle and lost; here there is no ark in view at all, only repentance and prayer, and God wins the battle. The chapter completes Samuel's portrait as the last and in some ways greatest of the judges, a prophet, priest, and deliverer. It also sets up the next crisis. If God has given victory through Samuel, why will Israel ask for a king in chapter 8?
historical:
The twenty years at Kiriath-jearim cover the period between the ark's return and the assembly at Mizpah. The ark remained there, apart from Israel's worship, until David brought it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), which would make the full period considerably longer than twenty years; the figure here marks the time until Israel's repentance, not the ark's entire stay.

Mizpah, whose name means watchtower, was a town in the territory of Benjamin, usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, a few miles north of Jerusalem. It served as a gathering place for the tribes (Judges 20:1). Samuel's yearly circuit took him to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah before returning to his home at Ramah, a fairly compact region in the central hill country, which suggests that his direct judicial role was centered there rather than across the whole land. The Amorites of verse 14 is a general term for the older inhabitants of the hill country of Canaan.
cultural:
The Baals and Ashtoreths were the chief male and female deities of Canaanite religion. Baal was a storm and fertility god believed to bring rain and crops; Ashtoreth (known elsewhere as Astarte) was a goddess associated with fertility and war. For farmers dependent on rain, worshiping them alongside the LORD seemed prudent, which is why Israel kept falling into it. Samuel demands that the people serve the LORD only.

The ceremony at Mizpah includes a ritual found nowhere else in the Old Testament as part of an assembly of repentance: drawing water and pouring it out before the LORD. (David later pours out water before the LORD in 2 Samuel 23:16, but in a different setting.) Its meaning is uncertain. Some see it as a sign of repentance and humility, like pouring out the heart (Lamentations 2:19); others think it symbolized the people's helplessness or a renunciation of the past. Fasting was a common sign of mourning and repentance. The whole burnt offering was entirely consumed on the altar, symbolizing total dedication. Setting up a memorial stone to mark an event where God acted was an old custom in Israel (Genesis 28:18; Joshua 4).
literary: The chapter works as a model story of repentance and deliverance, echoing the pattern of the book of Judges: the people turn from other gods, cry out, and God raises up a deliverer. But it differs from Judges in one striking way. There is no military hero. Samuel's weapons are prayer and sacrifice, and the battle is won by the LORD's thunder while Samuel is still offering the burnt offering. The chapter also answers chapter 4 point by point. There Israel was defeated at Ebenezer; here a stone called Ebenezer marks a victory. There the ark was used as a weapon; here the people seek the LORD himself. The closing verses (15-17) summarize Samuel's career as judge in the style of the Judges formulas, as though bringing an era to a close.

outline.t: The ark at Kiriath-jearim; twenty years of mourning
Samuel calls Israel to put away foreign gods
The LORD thunders, and the Philistines are routed
Peace in Samuel's days; his circuit as judge

doctrines.note: Samuel defines repentance as returning to the LORD with the whole heart, shown by removing rival gods and serving him only. The people's confession, “We have sinned against the LORD” (verse 6), is simple and direct. Repentance here is not a feeling but a turning, with concrete actions.

The people ask Samuel not to stop crying out to the LORD for them, and the LORD answers. Samuel's role as intercessor, praying on behalf of the nation, becomes one of his defining traits (see 12:23), and Jeremiah later names Samuel alongside Moses as a great intercessor (Jeremiah 15:1).

Israel cannot serve the LORD and the Baals together. The chapter treats putting away the foreign gods as the necessary first step before any deliverance, because divided loyalty is the root of Israel's trouble.

words.note: Even ha-ezer, Ebenezer, stone of help. The name first appeared in chapter 4 as the site of Israel's defeat. Here Samuel gives the name to a stone he sets up to mark victory. Since the two places seem to be different, the naming may be a deliberate reversal: the place-name of Israel's disgrace becomes a memorial of God's help.

Azar, to help. Samuel's explanation of the stone uses this verb: thus far the LORD has helped us. The phrase thus far can refer to place (up to this point on the map) or time (until now), and both senses may be intended. The related noun ezer, help, is used of God throughout the Psalms, as when the psalmist says his help comes from the LORD (Psalm 121:1-2).

Shaphat, to judge. In the Old Testament the word covers more than deciding legal cases; it means to rule, govern, and set things right. The judges of the book of Judges were deliverers and leaders. Samuel judges Israel at Mizpah and on his circuit, combining the roles of legal arbiter, spiritual leader, and deliverer.

Shaphakh, to pour out. Hannah had poured out her soul before the LORD (1:15), and now the people pour out water before him. The verb connects the private prayer of Samuel's mother with the public repentance of the nation her son leads.

christ: Samuel appears here as a mediator who prays for the people and offers sacrifice on their behalf, and God answers. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), who always lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25) and who offered himself as the once-for-all sacrifice. Samuel's intercession at Mizpah is not a prediction of Christ, but it belongs to the Old Testament pattern of intercessors (Abraham, Moses, Samuel) who stood between God and a sinful people, a pattern the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus. The chapter's movement from confession of sin, to sacrifice, to deliverance by God's own action also mirrors the shape of the gospel.

hard.q: If the Philistines were subdued all the days of Samuel, why are they still dominating Israel a few chapters later?
hard.a: Verse 13 says the Philistines stopped invading Israel's territory and that the LORD's hand was against them all Samuel's days, yet in chapters 9, 10, and 13 there are Philistine garrisons in Israel's land and the Philistines control the making of iron weapons. Interpreters handle this in several ways. Some understand verse 13 to mean that the Philistines made no further major invasions in Samuel's time as judge, while local garrisons and pressure continued. Others note that Samuel's active leadership gave way to Saul's, and the renewed Philistine threat belongs to Saul's reign, when Samuel was old. Many critical scholars think the chapter comes from a source that idealized Samuel's era, set alongside other sources with a different picture. Readers across these views agree that the chapter's purpose is theological: it shows what deliverance looks like when Israel repents and relies on the LORD, in contrast to the king-centered deliverance Israel will soon demand.

questions: Samuel told the people that returning to God meant getting rid of their rival gods. What would returning to God with your whole heart require you to put away?
The people asked Samuel not to stop praying for them. Who prays for you, and for whom do you pray consistently?
“Thus far the LORD has helped us.” What moments in your life might deserve a marker like the Ebenezer stone?
